item.title: When Botox Masks More Than Wrinkles
item.description:
Cognition

When Botox Masks More Than Wrinkles

Facial Botox has linguistic implications in American Sign Language.

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • In American Sign Language (ASL), facial movement conveys emotion and carries grammatical meaning.
  • Botox targets the same muscles ASL signers use for both emotional and grammatical expression.
  • Facial paralysis from Botox can weaken or blur grammatical markers like questions and negation.

Most people think of Botox as a wrinkle treatment with, at worst, a side effect of looking "frozen." But for the roughly half a million Americans who use American Sign Language (ASL), a frozen brow isn't a cosmetic quirk — it can be a communication problem. In ASL, the face is grammar.

The Face Talks Twice

Like hearing people, deaf signers use their faces to broadcast emotion — a raised brow of surprise, a soft smile of warmth.1,2 These affective expressions are largely universal, the same ones facial-feedback researchers study when they inject Botox into hearing subjects and track amygdala activity.3,4

However, ASL asks the face to do a second job simultaneously. Layered on top of these emotional signals is a completely separate system of grammatical facial movements, linguistic expression. Raised eyebrows with a forward head tilt mark a yes/no question; furrowed brows and a head shake mark a wh-question ("who," "what," "where"); other configurations mark conditionals, topics, or negation.1,5 Researchers call these "nonmanual markers," and they're every bit as rule-governed as verb conjugation in English.1,6

The Same Hands, a Different Sentence

Here's what surprises hearing people: identical hand signs can mean entirely different things depending on what the face does.5 Signing "Marry You" with neutral brows is a statement. Raising the eyebrows and leaning in converts this into a question: "Are you getting married?" Adding a head shake inverts the meaning into a negation. The hands never change, but the sentence does.

Deaf signers process linguistic facial expressions using dedicated neural machinery. Studies find grammatical facial markers activate the left hemisphere, the classic seat of language, while purely emotional expressions activate both hemispheres.7,8 Signers are also unusually sensitive to small differences in these cues, because a slightly different eyebrow position can be the difference between a statement and a question.7

If you want a gut-level sense of what's at stake, think about inflection in spoken English. "You're going to the party" and "You're going to the party?" use the exact same words — the only difference is the pitch rising at the end. Sarcasm, sincerity, and doubt can all ride on tone of voice while the words stay fixed. Now imagine your ability to raise or lower your pitch was limited. You could still say the words, but a listener would lose a whole layer of meaning underneath them.

This is roughly the relationship between ASL hand signs and facial grammar. While manual components such as hands and arms articulate the majority of content words, the face provides necessary syntactic and grammatical information.

What Neuromodulators Change

In aesthetic medicine, neuromodulators such as Botox and Dysport are used to smooth wrinkles and provide a more youthful appearance. Botox is often injected into the glabellar complex (a group of muscles used to form frown lines), the forehead, and the crow's feet (“laughter lines”), precisely the muscles ASL recruits for emotional and grammatical expression alike.9 Research shows that paralyzing these muscles changes not just how a person looks, but how well they broadcast emotion and how accurately others read it back, consistent with the facial feedback hypothesis.9-11 For a signer, a brow that can't fully furrow may weaken a wh-question until it reads as a statement, and a forehead that can't lift may blur "I'm going home" into "Am I going home?"

article continues after advertisement

Why This Belongs in the Counseling Room

None of this makes Botox off-limits for signers; many may adapt by leaning on additional manual signs, using body enactment, or modifying signage. What it does suggest is that the conversation between clinician and patient benefits from being broader. This highlights the distinction between an aesthetic trade-off and a linguistic trade-off from the same treatment in two different people. So, indeed, Botox treatments may influence signed communication and to some extent result in miscommunication. The higher the context, the less likely the miscommunication.

Clinicians have already built this type of individualized thinking into care for other populations. For example, patients with synkinesis have involuntary, cross-wired facial movements and require precise treatments that consider how facial movements convey emotional and social meaning. Extending that same lens to signing patients is less about limiting treatment than about ensuring that the full picture — cosmetic, emotional, and communicative — is part of an informed, collaborative decision.

item.title: Daily Cannabis Use Is at a Record High Among Young Adults
item.description:
Cannabis

Daily Cannabis Use Is at a Record High Among Young Adults

Teen cannabis risk rises with early use, higher THC potency, and frequent use.

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • New data show that daily or near-daily cannabis use among adults ages 19–30 reached an all-time high in 2025.
  • Adolescent-onset use occurs while reward, stress, emotional, and executive-control circuits are developing.
  • Early age of use, high-potency THC, easy access, and frequent or daily exposure are greatest concerns.

A few days after the newest Monitoring the Future annual data were released, Lantie Jorandby, MD, a former University of Florida College of Medicine mentee, called me. Jorandby is a founder, CEO, and lead psychiatrist at Canopy Pines Recovery, a women’s-only residential program for addiction and co-occurring mental illness. She was concerned about increasing numbers of women with cannabis use disorder and polysubstance dependence. Often, cannabis was not the only drug. Cannabis is frequently a part of a complicated psychiatric and polydrug clinical picture that often includes nicotine, alcohol, opioids, stimulants, and misuse of prescribed medications.

National data confirm Jorandby’s concerns. Young women use cannabis at about the same rate as young men. Daily cannabis use in young adults has reached a historic high, and cannabis and nicotine vaping remain extraordinarily common. I recently reported daily cannabis use at an all-time high.

When discussing daily marijuana use, it’s important to understand that THC exposure is not just a series of individual intoxications. The brain responds to repeated use by changing, and the brain on daily cannabis is not the same as the brain before use started.

Daily Use Is the Real Story

In 2025, 41.9 percent of young adults ages 19–30 reported cannabis use in the preceding year, and 28.8 percent used in the past month. The most important number, however, was 11.8 percent.

Nearly one in eight young adults (11.8 percent) reported cannabis use on at least 20 occasions in the preceding 30 days—the Monitoring the Future definition of daily or near-daily use. It was the highest level ever recorded and substantially increased from 6.9 percent in 2015. Daily cannabis use exceeds daily alcohol use among young adults.

Cannabis Use, 2015, 2020, and 2025
Source: Mark Gold, MD, with permission

The 2025 Monitoring the Future data report that daily, or near-daily, cannabis use among eighth graders was unchanged from 2024. Even this relatively low prevalence represents tens of thousands of predominantly 13- and 14-year-olds beginning frequent THC exposure during a sensitive brain neurodevelopmental period.

article continues after advertisement

Age matters too, as adolescent users have 2-3 times the risk of developing cannabis use disorder compared with people beginning use in adulthood. It's not just legalization and access but adult use of cannabis, trends, and beliefs that are at work here. The adult data I reported recently estimated that 21.4 million Americans ages 12 and older used cannabis daily or near-daily, compared with 19.9 million who smoked cigarettes daily. Daily or near-daily cannabis use had risen from approximately 17.7 million in 2022.

Daily Cannabis Use Rises Sharply
Source: Mark Gold, MD with permission

The Three-Part Risk Stack

In a 2026 American Journal of Psychiatry article, Kevin Hill and I argued that substance exposure should be understood across an extended neurodevelopmental window extending into the 30s.

Yasmin Hurd’s 2025 translational review makes the implications of cannabis especially clear. Risk is concentrated where three factors meet:

  1. Early initiation: Use begins while reward, emotional, and stress-regulation circuits are developing.
  2. THC dose: Flower containing roughly 2–4 percent THC has been replaced by THC products exceeding 15 percent.
  3. Frequent or daily use: Repeated THC dosing gives the developing brain less time to recover and return to normal.
article continues after advertisement

Hurd’s findings don’t prove every adolescent cannabis user is harmed. But chronic use affects attention and impulsivity, educational underachievement, anxiety, depression, cannabis use disorder, and psychosis-related outcomes. The most consistent cognitive effects occur in heavy or frequent users and with high-potency products.

In a "one dose matters” study by Hurd, adolescent rats exposed to a high THC dose comparable to modern products later showed more risky decision-making and impulsive behaviors compared to lower doses.

Persistent Doesn’t Necessarily Mean Permanent

The developing brain’s plasticity cuts both ways. It may make adolescent circuits more vulnerable to repeated THC exposure but also affords an opportunity for recovery. Hurd emphasizes that not all observed brain changes continue into adulthood and that changes are potentially reversible. Persistent change should therefore not be confused with inevitable, irreversible damage.

Addiction is the brain doing what it does best: learning—whether good or bad—through repetition and adaptation. Repeated drug exposure is altering what the brain expects and how it regulates reward, stress, sleep, and emotion. But prevention and early treatment can succeed as the brain remains highly capable of changing back again.

Women and Pregnancy

Young women have caught up to young men in cannabis use. In 2025, past-year cannabis use was approximately 42 percent among both young men and young women, with no statistically significant difference by sex. But equal prevalence does not mean equal risks. According to Jorandby, “Women differ in consequences from use and the development of SUDs. They also may have a more rapid progression from use to dependence. We see important differences in psychiatric vulnerabilities and co-occurring disorders too in these young women patients. Also, there are cannabis use and pregnancy risks, as these 19–30-year-old women are in their peak childbearing years.”

article continues after advertisement

Major medical organizations recommend avoiding cannabis during pregnancy and breastfeeding. THC crosses the placenta and transfers into breast milk. Because the fetal endocannabinoid system participates in brain connectivity and circuit formation, prenatal exposure is a significant public health concern.

Nicotine Plus Cannabis and Vaping Devices

Recent Monitoring the Future declines in cigarette smoking, alcohol use, and binge drinking are important to note but should not obscure the unacceptably high number of daily cannabis users, high-potency young THC users, and combined nicotine–cannabis vapers. Some have blamed the lack of enforcement at marijuana shops, but regardless of how, in 2025, 15.1 percent of young adults vaped cannabis during the past month. Past-30-day nicotine vaping among young adults has approximately tripled since it was first measured in 2017, reaching 19.3 percent in 2025. Past-year nicotine vaping reached 24.8 percent, nearly twice its 2017 prevalence. Past-year nicotine-pouch use among young adults more than doubled from 2023 to 2025, reaching 12.7 percent, although the increase from 9.5 percent in 2024 was not statistically significant. Monitoring the Future reports these behaviors separately, but nicotine and cannabis increasingly travel together.

Vaping devices are discreet, portable, rapidly reinforcing, and capable of quickly delivering concentrated drugs to the brain. Frequent redosing is easy, and dependence becomes harder for families, teachers, and clinicians to recognize. There is little odor, little preparation, and no obvious stopping point, unlike finishing a cigarette or joint. All this is increasing cannabis use disorder problems. Parents should not simply ask whether a child smokes marijuana but also ask about vaping, gummies, beverages, and concentrates.

Prevention

The adolescent brain is vulnerable and in flux, so prevention is ideal. If prevention fails, early intervention can change the trajectory. The honest message is neither “cannabis is harmless” nor “every user is damaged.” Youth sports and other healthy alternatives support the brain's development while strengthening resilience, social connection, and well-being. Successful prevention strategies aim to discuss the healthy, drug-free brain and the differences between developing people and adults. CADCA utilizes science-based evidence showing that the adolescent brain is under construction and substance use directly disrupts critical neurodevelopment. They support early and frequent screening and prompt treatment of SUDs that emerge.
